note.explanation: Atoms have a tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus. A shell farther from the nucleus has greater energy. Modern science describes electron locations in terms of probability, rather than exact paths.
examples: A proton has a positive charge, an electron has a negative charge, and a neutron has no charge.
For the third shell, n = 3, so the maximum number of electrons is 2 × 3² = 18.
note.checkAnswer: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, held together by strong nuclear force.
note.simple: An atom is like a very tiny centre with electrons around it: the centre is the nucleus, and the electrons occupy energy shells.

written.text: What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?
written.finalAnswer: In Bohr's model, an electron revolves around the nucleus in a specific orbit or shell with fixed energy. The modern approach describes electrons as charged clouds and their locations as probabilities, so their exact paths and locations cannot be predicted with complete certainty.

written.text: During discharge tube experiments, how did the scientists conclude that the same type of electrons and protons are present in all the elements?

The presence of positive particles was also observed, and Rutherford showed that the hydrogen nucleus, or proton, is present in other nuclei.

explain.title: The atom has a central nucleus
explain.body: The nucleus is a tiny central portion of the atom. It contains protons and neutrons, which are held together by strong nuclear force. Almost all the atom's mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

explain.title: Electrons occupy shells
explain.body: In Bohr's model, electrons can revolve in specific orbits called shells. Each shell has a fixed energy. The first shell is nearest to the nucleus and has the lowest energy; shells farther away have greater energy.

explain.title: The modern view describes probability
explain.body: The modern approach does not give an electron a precisely known path. It describes electrons as charged clouds and tells us the probability of finding an electron in a region.

explain.title: Calculate shell capacity
explain.body: Use the formula 2n², where n is the shell number. For example, for n = 3, 2 × 3² = 18, so the third shell can accommodate at most 18 electrons.

mistakes: Do not put electrons in the nucleus; electrons occupy the extra-nuclear region.
Do not confuse the proton's positive charge with the electron's negative charge.
Do not say all shells have equal energy; shells farther from the nucleus have greater energy.
When using 2n², square n before multiplying by 2.
Do not describe the modern view as giving an electron a precisely known path; it gives a probability of finding the electron.
